title: What is thread starvation: some threads never get CPU time because other threads hold locks too long or there are too few threads in the pool: diagnose via thread dump showing many WAITING/BLOCKED threads?

s1_definition.oneliner: Starvation is threads that never get their turn because others hog the CPU or locks, or the pool is too small; a thread dump full of WAITING/BLOCKED threads reveals it.
s1_definition.profdef: Thread starvation is when a thread is perpetually denied the resources it needs to make progress – usually CPU time or a lock – because other threads monopolize them. It happens when some threads hold locks far too long, when higher-priority threads crowd out lower-priority ones, or when a thread pool is too small so tasks queue up and effectively never run in time. You diagnose it from a thread dump that shows many threads stuck in WAITING or BLOCKED states while only a few threads hold resources or run.

sections.s2_detail:
### What is thread starvation?

Starvation comes from a few distinct causes. The first is long-held locks: if one thread holds a lock while doing slow work, like a network call or a big computation, every other thread that needs that lock is blocked and starves. The fix is to shorten the critical section, only holding the lock for the minimal state change and doing slow work outside it. The second cause is an undersized thread pool: if you have a pool of, say, ten threads but hundreds of tasks that each block on I/O, all ten threads get stuck waiting and new tasks queue indefinitely, so they are effectively starved of a thread to run on. The fix is to size the pool correctly for the workload, or to avoid blocking inside pooled threads.

### How does thread starvation work?

A particularly nasty variant is thread-pool deadlock by starvation: if tasks in a bounded pool submit sub-tasks to the same pool and then wait for them, all threads can end up waiting for sub-tasks that can never start because no thread is free to run them. The pool is not technically deadlocked on locks, but it makes no progress, which is a starvation-induced hang. The fix is to never block a pooled thread on work that must run in the same pool, or to use separate pools.

### Why does this matter?

To diagnose starvation, you take a thread dump and look at the distribution of thread states. If you see many threads in WAITING (parked, waiting on a condition or a pool's work queue) or BLOCKED (waiting for a lock) while only one or a few threads are RUNNABLE holding resources, that pattern points to starvation. For a pool, you look at how many pool threads are idle-waiting on the queue versus how deep the queue is; a growing queue with all workers blocked is the signature. Metrics like thread-pool active count, queue size, and task latency make this obvious on a dashboard.

### How do you use this in practice?

A senior nuance: distinguish starvation from deadlock and livelock. In deadlock, specific threads are BLOCKED on each other forever in a cycle. In starvation, threads could run if they got a turn, but they keep being passed over. Fairness helps – a `ReentrantLock(true)` is a fair lock that grants access in arrival order, preventing a thread from being skipped indefinitely, at some throughput cost. You also prevent starvation with proper pool sizing (often using Little's Law to pick the size from throughput and latency), bounded queues with sensible rejection policies, and separating fast and slow work into different pools so a slow task cannot starve fast ones.

### What are the rules and constraints?

sections.s6_takeaway:
Thread starvation is when a thread is perpetually denied what it needs to make progress, usually CPU time or a lock, because other threads monopolize those resources. It is different from deadlock: in a deadlock specific threads are blocked on each other in a cycle forever, but in starvation the threads could run perfectly well if they ever got a turn, they just keep being passed over. The common causes are locks held far too long while a thread does slow work, higher-priority threads crowding out lower-priority ones, and, most often in my experience, a thread pool that is too small, so tasks pile up in the queue and effectively never get a thread to run on in time.

I diagnose it from a thread dump by looking at the distribution of thread states. The signature is many threads sitting in WAITING or BLOCKED, parked on a lock or on a pool's work queue, while only a few threads are actually running and holding the resources. For a thread pool specifically, I look at the active worker count against the queue depth: if every worker is busy and the queue just keeps growing, the waiting tasks are being starved. Pool metrics like active count, queue size, and task latency make this obvious on a dashboard.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this bit us in the payment service. We had a thread pool of only a couple of threads, and under load hundreds of transfer tasks arrived, each making a slow downstream call, so all the pool threads stayed busy on slow work and everything else queued. The real pain was that quick balance checks were submitted to the same pool and got stuck behind the slow transfers, so a thirty-second-equivalent quick lookup was waiting seconds. I fixed it two ways: first I sized the pool correctly for the real throughput and latency using Little's Law instead of guessing, and second I applied the bulkhead pattern by giving fast operations their own separate pool so a slow transfer could never starve a quick balance check again. Where ordering fairness mattered, I also used a fair ReentrantLock so no thread could be skipped indefinitely. Separating fast and slow work into different pools is the single most effective habit I have for preventing starvation.

Remember one sentence: What is thread starvation: some threads never get CPU time because other threads hold locks too long or there are too few threads in the pool: diagnose via thread dump showing many WAITING/BLOCKED threads is fundamental knowledge for Java interviews and production banking work.

---

keyPoints: A thread never gets CPU time because higher-priority threads dominate
Differs from deadlock: threads are not blocked, just never scheduled
Cause: unfair locks, thread priority abuse, long-running synchronized blocks
Detection: thread dump shows threads in RUNNABLE but making no progress
Fix: fair locks (new ReentrantLock(true)), shorter critical sections
